scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Circassian dance originates from the North Caucasus, home to the Circassian people before the 19th-century Circassian genocide.
It reflects the martial lifestyle and social customs of the region, with historical records from the 19th century describing competition dances that served as physical training and social display.
The tradition continues today in diaspora communities in Turkey, Jordan, Israel, and Russia, preserved through festivals and education.
on_screen: Map: Russia (North Caucasus), Turkey, Jordan, Israel · Central Asia
Image 1 with attribution

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Circassian dances are performed at weddings, social gatherings, national festivals, and ritual occasions.
They serve as social communication, courtship, and displays of martial skill and endurance.
Some dances have ritual origins honoring deities or marking seasonal events.
Today it is a living tradition.
on_screen: Footage — MISSING (use images)

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: Circassian dances include mass circle formations (Wuj), slow partner dances (Qafa), and fast-paced pair dances (Islamey).
Men often dance on the tips of their toes wearing special leather boots, performing agile leaps and turned-in foot positions with hands behind their backs in competition styles.
Women glide lightly with motionless upper bodies and heads, moving smoothly on half-toes without touching partners in Qafa.
Watch for Zakladka, Toe dancing, Do-za-do.
on_screen: Hero video — MISSING
Captions name each signature move as it appears
Formation: Mass circle dances moving counter-clockwise; partner dances maintain respectful distance without touching; solo male performances in center

scenes.title: Listen
narration: Circassian dance music features instruments such as the pshine accordion, pkhachich clappers (wood blocks), bereban drum (dhol), pkhetaw (wood-strike), shichepshin fiddle (horse-tail violin), apa-pshine lute, and qamil flute.
Rhythms are typically in 4/4 or 8/4 meters, with pieces like Qaashuo and Zefauk in 4/4 time.
Listen for the pshine accordion, pkhachich clappers, bereban drum, pkhetaw wood-strike.
The pulse is 4/4 8/4 at about 70 beats a minute.

The music features a blend of accordion melodies, rhythmic clapping on wooden blocks, deep drum beats, and high-pitched fiddle lines, creating a dynamic soundscape that supports both slow, dignified dances and fast, energetic performances.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Men wear the cherkes, a black military-style outfit with an imposing coat and bullet cartridges across the chest, often carrying a dagger or sword incorporated into dances.
Women wear elegant dresses that emphasize grace and lightness of movement.
Performances occur at national festivals, weddings, and cultural celebrations, often on flat indoor or outdoor stages suitable for circle and partner formations.
on_screen: Image gallery: 5 licensed images with attribution
Reconstruction imagery allowed only from the costume notes, labelled 'reconstruction'

scenes.title: The people
narration: Notable Circassian musicians and composers include Hapcha Zaodin, Hasan Sokov, Aslan Leiv (Aslan Dudar), and Aslan Tlebzu.
Diaspora artists include Saeed Bazoqa and Ahmad Aiy.
Variants include the Kabardian and Bzhedug versions of Islamey, differing in tempo and style.
Circassian dance influenced neighboring cultures, notably Cossack dance.
on_screen: Names on screen as they are spoken
Variant names as a small list

scenes.title: Family tree
narration: Circassian dance is sibling of Lezginka: Distinct but related Caucasian dance; Circassian dance influenced and differs from Lezginka, which is from the Lezghi people.
Circassian dance is influence of Cossack dance: Circassian dance traditions historically influenced the development of Cossack dance.
